claim: Rod photoreceptors contribute to vision across a million-fold range of light intensities.
source: Rod photoreceptors contribute to vision across a million-fold range of light intensities.
evidence: This is a general statement about rod photoreceptor function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Work in mouse shows that rod photoreceptor signals are routed through several retinal pathways, each specialized for different light levels.
source: For example, work in mouse shows that rod photoreceptor signals are routed through several retinal pathways, each specialized for different light levels.
evidence: This claim references prior work in mouse retina, implying citation of previous studies.

claim: Light-level-dependent routing of rod signals has been invoked to explain several human perceptual results.
source: This light-level-dependent routing of rod signals has been invoked to explain several human perceptual results, but it has not been tested in primate retina.
evidence: This statement references the scientific literature where this hypothesis has been proposed.

claim: Rod signals traverse the primate retina almost exclusively through a single pathway – the dedicated rod bipolar pathway.
source: Here, we show, surprisingly, that rod signals traverse the primate retina almost exclusively through a single pathway – the dedicated rod bipolar pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are substantial differences in how rod signals traverse the retina between mouse and primate.
source: Identical experiments in mouse and primate reveal substantial differences in how rod signals traverse the retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative experimental data from both species presented in the manuscript.

claim: The speeding of rod signals with light level is inherited directly from the rod photoreceptors themselves rather than from different pathways with distinct kinetics.
source: This includes a prominent speeding of rod signals with light level – which we show is inherited directly from the rod photoreceptors themselves rather than from different pathways with distinct kinetics.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements of rod photoreceptor kinetics.

claim: In starlight, photons are few and far between, and retinal circuits face the considerable challenge of detecting and reliably transmitting signals resulting from the absorption of individual photons.
source: At the low end of this range - for example in starlight - photons are few and far between, and retinal circuits face the considerable challenge of detecting and reliably transmitting signals resulting from the absorption of individual photons (reviewed by (Field et al., 2005; Takeshita et al., 2017)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The high gain associated with detecting single photons, if unabated, would quickly saturate retinal responses in moonlight.
source: For example, in moonlight the high gain associated with detecting single photons, if unabated, would quickly saturate retinal responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of retinal signal processing.

claim: A prominent hypothesis proposes that the routes that rod-derived signals take through the retina depend on mean light level.
source: A prominent hypothesis about how retinal circuits meet these changing demands proposes that the routes that rod-derived signals take through the retina depend on mean light level (Sharpe and Stockman, 1999; Tsukamoto et al., 2001; Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001; Deans et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Different retinal circuits are specialized to handle the challenges associated with different light levels.
source: A prominent hypothesis about how retinal circuits meet these changing demands proposes that the routes that rod-derived signals take through the retina depend on mean light level (Sharpe and Stockman, 1999; Tsukamoto et al., 2001; Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001; Deans et al., 2002) - with different circuits specialized to handle the challenges associated with different light levels.
evidence: This is part of the hypothesis described in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: In the primary pathway, dedicated rod bipolar cells transmit rod signals.
source: These circuits include (Figure 1; reviewed by (Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001; Field et al., 2005; Field and Chichilnisky, 2007; Demb and Singer, 2012)): (1) the primary pathway, in which dedicated rod bipolar cells transmit rod signals
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In the secondary pathway, gap junctions convey rod signals to cones and the associated cone circuitry.
source: (2) the secondary pathway, in which gap junctions convey rod signals to cones and the associated cone circuitry
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In the tertiary pathway, Off cone bipolar cell dendrites receive direct rod input.
source: (3) the tertiary pathway, in which Off cone bipolar cell dendrites receive direct rod input.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Rod signals can reach cones (and then cone bipolar cells) through horizontal cells, creating rod-cone spectral opponency.
source: Recent work also proposes that rod signals can reach cones (and then cone bipolar cells) through horizontal cells, creating rod-cone spectral opponency (Joesch and Meister, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Light steps producing ~40 R*/rod/s halved the outer segment current in primate rods.
source: Light steps producing ~40 R*/rod/s halved the outer segment current, and steps producing ≥300 R*/rod/s suppressed nearly all of the dark current.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from suction electrode recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Light steps producing ≥300 R*/rod/s suppressed nearly all of the dark current in primate rods.
source: Light steps producing ~40 R*/rod/s halved the outer segment current, and steps producing ≥300 R*/rod/s suppressed nearly all of the dark current.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from suction electrode recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mean backgrounds of 250 R*/rod/s suppressed 90% of the dark current in primate rods.
source: Mean backgrounds of 250 R*/rod/s suppressed 90% of the dark current (red line).
evidence: This is a measurement from multiple experiments summarized in Figure 2B.

claim: The suppression of rod dark current was maintained during light steps that persisted for 2–3 min with less than 5% recovery.
source: This suppression was maintained during light steps that persisted for 2–3 min (<5% recovery of dark current, not shown).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the authors' data.

claim: Between darkness and 3 R*/rod/s, RGC gain declined considerably more than rod gain.
source: Between darkness and 3 R*/rod/s, RGC gain declined considerably more than rod gain.
evidence: This is a finding from the data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The reduction in RGC gain between darkness and 3 R*/rod/s reflects post-rod circuit adaptation.
source: This reduction in RGC gain reflects post-rod circuit adaptation (Lee et al., 1990; Purpura et al., 1990; Dunn et al., 2006; Schwartz and Rieke, 2013)
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: For backgrounds between 3 and 100 R*/rod/s, both rod and ganglion cell gain declined approximately inversely with background, as expected for Weber's Law.
source: For backgrounds between 3 and 100 R*/rod/s, both rod and ganglion cell gain declined approximately inversely with background, as expected for Weber's Law (reviewed in (Rieke and Rudd, 2009)).
evidence: This is a finding from the data in Figure 2D, with reference to established theory.

claim: Above 100 R*/rod/s, rod signal gain in both rods and RGCs declined with increasing background more sharply than expected from Weber's Law, falling by a factor of ~100 between 100 and 1000 R*/rod/s.
source: Above 100 R*/rod/s, rod signal gain in both rods and RGCs declined with increasing background more sharply than expected from Weber's Law, falling by a factor of ~100 between 100 and 1000 R*/rod/s (black line).
evidence: This is a finding from the data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The abrupt decline in the gain of rod-derived signals coincides closely with the suppression of outer segment current.
source: This abrupt decline in the gain of rod-derived signals coincides closely with the suppression of outer segment current (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing data in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: The primary limitation on the range of rod-derived signaling in the retinal output is a decrease in the gain of rod signals, rather than decreased gain in post-rod circuitry.
source: These experiments indicate that the primary limitation on the range of rod-derived signaling in the retinal output is a decrease in the gain of rod signals, rather than decreased gain in post-rod circuitry.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Rods may continue to weakly modulate retinal output signals above 300 R*/rod/s, as observed in rodents.
source: Rods may continue to weakly modulate retinal output signals above 300 R*/rod/s, as observed in rodents (Yin et al., 2006; Naarendorp et al., 2010; Tikidji-Hamburyan et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on observations in other species, supported by citations.

claim: AII amacrine cells receive direct glutamatergic input from rod bipolar cells through AMPA-type glutamate receptors.
source: AII amacrines receive direct glutamatergic input from rod bipolar cells through AMPA-type glutamate receptors and make bidirectional electrical synapses with On cone bipolar cell axons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: AII amacrine cells make bidirectional electrical synapses with On cone bipolar cell axons.
source: AII amacrines receive direct glutamatergic input from rod bipolar cells through AMPA-type glutamate receptors and make bidirectional electrical synapses with On cone bipolar cell axons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Under control conditions, AII responses reflect signaling from both the primary pathway via rod bipolar cells and the secondary pathway via gap junctional input from cone bipolar cells.
source: Thus, under control conditions, AII responses reflect signaling from both the primary pathway via rod bipolar cells and the secondary pathway via gap junctional input from cone bipolar cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known anatomy and physiology of AII amacrine cells.

claim: In the presence of AMPA receptor antagonists, remaining AII responses reflect input only from the secondary pathway.
source: In the presence of AMPA receptor antagonists, remaining AII responses reflect input only from the secondary pathway (Cohen, 1998; Trexler et al., 2001; Murphy and Rieke, 2008; Münch et al., 2009; Grimes et al., 2014b; Ke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological approach supported by multiple citations.

claim: Block of AMPA receptors with NBQX reduced AII responses more than 80% at backgrounds at or below 30 R*/rod/s.
source: Block of AMPA receptors with NBQX reduced AII responses more than 80% at backgrounds at or below 30 R*/rod/s (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: NBQX-insensitive AII responses were largely absent over the range of light levels in which rods modulate the retinal outputs (i.e. below 300 R*/rod/s).
source: Most importantly for our purposes, NBQX-insensitive responses were largely absent over the range of light levels in which rods modulate the retinal outputs (i.e. below 300 R*/rod/s).
evidence: This is a finding from the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The correspondence between rod saturation and the emergence of NBQX-insensitive responses suggests that the secondary rod pathway does not play a major role in transmitting rod signals to ganglion cells in primates, regardless of light level.
source: This correspondence between rod saturation (Figure 2) and the emergence of NBQX-insensitive responses (Figure 3) suggests that the secondary rod pathway does not play a major role in transmitting rod signals to ganglion cells in primates, regardless of light level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: H1 horizontal cells receive direct synaptic input from L- and M- cones.
source: H1 horizontal cells receive direct synaptic input from L- and M- cones (Figure 3A; [Kolb, 1970; Rodieck, 1998; Verweij et al., 1999]).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rod input could reach H1 horizontal cells through rod-cone gap junctions and cone synaptic output.
source: Rod input could reach H1 horizontal cells through rod-cone gap junctions and cone synaptic output (Nelson, 1977; Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1995; Hornstein et al., 2005)
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Rod input could reach H1 horizontal cells through direct rod contacts onto H1 cells as suggested by recent work in mouse.
source: or through direct rod contacts onto H1 cells as suggested by recent work in mouse (Joesch and Meister, 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on recent work in mouse, supported by citation.

claim: H1 horizontal cell responses were weak at low backgrounds but became pronounced at backgrounds ≥ 300 R*/rod/s.
source: H1 responses, like the NBQX-insensitive responses of AII amacrine cells, were weak at low backgrounds but became pronounced at backgrounds ≥ 300 R*/rod/s (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Cone responses were very similar to those of horizontal cells, with the emergence of a sizeable response only for backgrounds ≥ 300 R*/rod/s.
source: Responses of cones were very similar to those of horizontal cells, with the emergence of a sizeable response only for backgrounds ≥ 300 R*/rod/s (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The weak rod responses in cones and horizontal cells are consistent with the NBQX-insensitive responses in AII amacrine cells.
source: The weak rod responses in cones and horizontal cells are consistent with the NBQX-insensitive responses in AII amacrine cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing data across different cell types.

claim: The secondary pathway plays, at most, a minor role in transmitting rod signals to ganglion cells in primate retina for the stimuli probed.
source: Thus, these results collectively indicate that the secondary pathway plays, at most, a minor role in transmitting rod signals to ganglion cells in primate retina for the stimuli probed here.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Previous experiments in rodents have assigned a substantial role to the secondary pathway in transmitting rod signals.
source: The lack of prominent secondary pathway contributions in primate was unexpected, as previous experiments in rodents have assigned a substantial role to the secondary pathway in transmitting rod signals (Deans et al., 2002; Trexler et al., 2005; Grimes et al., 2014b; Ke et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work in rodents.

claim: Near-complete suppression of the outer segment current occurred at higher light levels in mouse compared to primate rods (90% saturation at 1000 vs 250 R*/rod/s).
source: Near-complete suppression of the outer segment current occurred at higher light levels in mouse compared to primate rods (90% saturation at 1000 vs 250 R*/rod/s; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of experimental measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The contrast sensitivity of signals in the secondary pathway in mouse was half maximal at ~5 R*/rod/s, nearly two orders of magnitude lower than the half-maximal intensity of secondary-pathway rod signals in primate.
source: Voltage responses of AII amacrine cells in NBQX (Figure 4B) and of horizontal cells in control conditions (Figure 4C–D) to fixed-contrast stimuli indicated that the contrast sensitivity of signals in the secondary pathway in mouse was half maximal at ~5 R*/rod/s, nearly two orders of magnitude lower than the half-maximal intensity of secondary-pathway rod signals in primate.
evidence: This is a finding from comparative experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Signaling in mouse and primate rod photoreceptors is much more similar than signaling in the circuits that convey rod signals to ganglion cells.
source: These experiments indicate that signaling in mouse and primate rod photoreceptors is much more similar than signaling in the circuits that convey rod signals to ganglion cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative data in Figure 4.

claim: The secondary pathway in mouse begins contributing to retinal output at light levels that are more than 100-fold below rod saturation.
source: Specifically, the secondary pathway in mouse begins contributing to retinal output at light levels that are more than 100-fold below rod saturation, whereas in primate signals from the secondary pathway are largely absent below rod saturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative data in Figure 4.

claim: In primate, signals from the secondary pathway are largely absent below rod saturation.
source: Specifically, the secondary pathway in mouse begins contributing to retinal output at light levels that are more than 100-fold below rod saturation, whereas in primate signals from the secondary pathway are largely absent below rod saturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Cone-derived responses were much larger than rod-derived responses at temporal frequencies ≥ 10 Hz.
source: As observed previously (Dacey, 2000), cone-derived responses were much larger than rod-derived responses at temporal frequencies ≥ 10 Hz (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 5B, consistent with previous work.

claim: Across all temporal frequencies that elicited clear rod responses (≤10 Hz), the ratio of H1 responses to rod- and cone-preferring stimuli was at least seven times smaller than that for On parasol responses to the same stimuli.
source: Across all temporal frequencies that elicited clear rod responses (≤10 Hz), the ratio of H1 responses to rod- and cone-preferring stimuli was at least seven times smaller than that for On parasol responses to the same stimuli (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data presented in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Rod-derived signals recorded in the secondary pathway in response to sinusoidal stimuli are too weak to explain rod-derived RGC responses.
source: Hence, rod-derived signals recorded in the secondary pathway in response to sinusoidal stimuli are too weak to explain rod-derived RGC responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 5.

claim: The primary rod pathway dominates responses to both sinusoidal and flashed stimuli.
source: Instead, the primary rod pathway dominates responses to both sinusoidal and flashed stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A perceptual observation shows unexpectedly low sensitivity to 15 Hz rod flicker over a specific luminance range.
source: A particular perceptual observation that motivates the rod routing hypothesis is an unexpectedly low sensitivity to 15 Hz rod flicker over a specific luminance range (Sharpe et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to perceptual work.

claim: A proposed explanation for the 15 Hz rod flicker null is that rod signals in slow and fast retinal circuits arrive at a downstream integration site out of phase and hence cancel.
source: A proposed explanation for this percept is that rod signals in slow and fast retinal circuits arrive at a downstream integration site out of phase and hence cancel (Sharpe and Stockman, 1999).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: On parasol responses to 15 Hz flicker increased monotonically without an apparent null or abrupt change in phase.
source: On parasol responses increased monotonically without an apparent null or abrupt change in phase needed to explain the perceptual observations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Temporal tuning of On parasol responses did not exhibit any abrupt discontinuities across the range of light levels suggestive of rod-rod cancelation.
source: In particular, temporal tuning did not exhibit any abrupt discontinuities across this range of light levels suggestive of rod-rod cancelation.
evidence: This is a finding from the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The perceptual flicker null does not originate from convergence of parallel rod circuits prior to On parasol RGCs.
source: This data suggests that the perceptual flicker null does not originate from convergence of parallel rod circuits prior to On parasol RGCs (see Discussion and Cao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, with reference to previous work.

claim: Rod signals could reach Off cone bipolar cells from three known sources: dendritic input directly from rods (tertiary pathway), dendritic input from cones (secondary pathway), and axonal inhibitory input from AII amacrine cells (primary pathway).
source: Rod signals could reach Off cone bipolar cells from three known sources (Figure 1): (1) dendritic input directly from rods (i.e. tertiary pathway), (2) dendritic input from cones (i.e. secondary pathway), and (3) axonal inhibitory input from AII amacrine cells (i.e. primary pathway).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In Off RGCs, responses to rod-preferring stimuli were roughly half as large as responses to cone-preferring stimuli at 20 R*/rod/s.
source: In Off RGCs, responses to rod-preferring stimuli were roughly half as large as responses to cone-preferring stimuli (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: The difference in the relative sensitivity of rod and cone signals indicates that rod signals are less strongly routed through Off cone bipolar cells than On cone bipolar cells at 20 R*/rod/s.
source: This difference in the relative sensitivity of rod and cone signals indicates in turn that rod signals are less strongly routed through Off cone bipolar cells than On cone bipolar cells at this light level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 6.

claim: The On/Off asymmetry in rod and cone signal weighting supports the conclusion that the secondary rod pathway does not convey strong rod-derived signals in primate.
source: The On/Off asymmetry supports the conclusion that the secondary rod pathway does not convey strong rod-derived signals in primate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 6.

claim: In the secondary pathway, rod- and cone-derived signals are mixed prior to transmission to On and Off bipolar cells; such mixing should lead to similar weighting in On and Off circuits.
source: In the secondary pathway, rod- and cone-derived signals are mixed prior to transmission to On and Off bipolar cells; such mixing should lead to similar weighting in On and Off circuits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known anatomy of the secondary pathway.

claim: Suppression of On pathways with LY/APB reduced responses to short wavelength stimuli in Off parasol cells more than 80% at backgrounds ≤ 20 R*/rod/s.
source: However, suppression of On pathways reduced responses to short wavelength stimuli in Off parasol cells more than 80% at backgrounds ≤ 20 R*/rod/s (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: LY/APB reduced Off parasol excitatory synaptic input by 20% at 200 R*/rod/s.
source: LY/APB reduced Off parasol excitatory synaptic input considerably less at higher light levels (20% reduction at 200 R*/rod/s).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Rod signals reach Off RGCs mainly through the primary rod pathway over most or all of the mesopic range.
source: Although these results are subject to the caveat that the pharmacology could have off-target affects, they suggest that rod signals reach Off RGCs mainly through the primary rod pathway over most or all of the mesopic range.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, with acknowledgment of potential caveats.

claim: At a background of 0.5 R*/rod/s in mouse, LY/APB reduced excitatory inputs to Off sustained alpha RGCs by ~90%, indicating that the primary pathway dominates signaling at this light level.
source: At a background of 0.5 R*/rod/s, LY/APB reduced excitatory inputs to Off sustained alpha RGCs by ~90%, indicating that the primary pathway dominates signaling at this light level.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from mouse retina shown in Figure 6G.

claim: At a background of 5 R*/rod/s in mouse, LY/APB reduced Off alpha RGC responses by 35%.
source: At a background of 5 R*/rod/s, LY/APB reduced responses by 35%, and at a background of 50 R*/rod/s, responses were little affected.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from mouse retina shown in Figure 6.

claim: At a background of 50 R*/rod/s in mouse, LY/APB had little effect on Off alpha RGC responses.
source: At a background of 5 R*/rod/s, LY/APB reduced responses by 35%, and at a background of 50 R*/rod/s, responses were little affected.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from mouse retina shown in Figure 6.

claim: The primary rod pathway provides the dominant route that rod-derived signals take through the primate retina across scotopic and mesopic light levels for a wide range of stimuli.
source: Collectively, the experiments in Figures 3–6 indicate a surprising difference between how rod signals traverse the mouse and primate retinas. Specifically, unlike the situation in mouse, the primary rod pathway provides the dominant route that rod-derived signals take through the primate retina across scotopic and mesopic light levels for a wide range of stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by data from Figures 3-6.

claim: The dominance of the primary pathway maximizes opportunities to independently process rod and cone signals since they are not mixed until late in the retinal circuitry.
source: This dominance of the primary pathway means that perceptual phenomena previously attributed to a change in routing need to be reinterpreted (e.g. section on kinetics below); it also maximizes opportunities to independently process rod and cone signals since they are not mixed until late in the retinal circuitry.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding of primary pathway dominance.

claim: Perceptual experiments show that the kinetics of rod-derived signals speed relative to cone-derived signals as light levels increase.
source: Perceptual experiments show that the kinetics of rod-derived signals speed relative to cone-derived signals as light levels increase (Sharpe et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to perceptual work.

claim: The speeding of rod-derived signals is often attributed to a luminance-dependent change in the dominant route that rod-derived signals take through the retina.
source: This speeding is often attributed to a luminance-dependent change in the dominant route that rod-derived signals take through the retina (reviewed by (Buck, 2004; Chen et al., 2000; Stockman and Sharpe, 2006; Buck, 2014))
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The shift in kinetics of rod-derived signals appears to originate within the rods themselves.
source: Instead, as described below, the shift in kinetics of rod-derived signals appears to originate within the rods themselves.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented later.

claim: Both spike responses and excitatory synaptic inputs of On parasol RGCs sped by ~100 ms across the range of light levels from 0.2 to 100 R*/rod/s.
source: Both spike responses and excitatory synaptic inputs sped by ~100 ms across the range of light levels probed (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Kinetic changes in RGC responses between 1 and 10 R*/rod/s were similar in magnitude to those measured in perceptual experiments.
source: Kinetic changes between 1 and 10 R*/rod/s were similar in magnitude to those measured in perceptual experiments (Sharpe et al., 1989), suggesting that the retina makes a substantial contribution to the speeding observed perceptually.
evidence: This is a comparison between the authors' data and perceptual data from the literature.

claim: The conserved routing of rod signals across light levels indicates that kinetic shifts occur within elements of the primary rod pathway rather than from a change in the dominant pathway.
source: The conserved routing of rod signals across these light levels indicates that these kinetic shifts occur within elements of the primary rod pathway rather than from a change in the dominant pathway conveying rod signals through the retina.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the routing data and kinetic measurements.

claim: The change in kinetics observed in rod phototransduction currents could account for ~40% of the change in kinetics observed in RGC responses.
source: Specifically, the change in kinetics observed in rod phototransduction currents could account for ~40% of the change in kinetics observed in RGC responses (Figure 7F, compare dashed blue line and closed circles).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data in Figure 7F.

claim: Rod voltage responses to brief flashes showed larger changes in kinetics than observed in the photocurrents.
source: Rod voltage responses (Figure 7E) to brief flashes showed larger changes in kinetics than observed in the photocurrents (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: Rod voltage responses to sinusoidal stimuli (predicted from flash responses) could fully explain the ~100 ms change in kinetics of RGC responses to sinusoidal stimuli.
source: Further, when we used the flash responses to predict responses to sinusoidal stimuli, we found that they could fully explain the ~100 ms change in kinetics of RGC responses to sinusoidal stimuli (Figure 7F, dashed blue line and open circles).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The speeding of the rod voltage response coincided with a large steady-state hyperpolarization of the rod membrane potential (9.0 ± 0.7 mV upon a step from 1 to 60 R*/rod/s).
source: The speeding of the rod voltage response coincided with a large steady-state hyperpolarization of the rod membrane potential (9.0 ± 0.7 mV upon a step from 1 to 60 R*/rod/s, n = 10; Figure 7G).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Hyperpolarization sped the rod membrane time constant by a factor of ~2.
source: Hyperpolarization indeed sped the membrane time constant by a factor of ~2 (Figure 7I), and this effect was well-matched to the physiological range of rod voltages (resting membrane potential in darkness of −44 ± 1 mV, n = 10).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The change in kinetics of the rod-derived retinal outputs originates largely from the rods themselves rather than from a light-dependent shift in the routing of rod signals through fast and slow retinal circuits.
source: These experiments indicate that the change in kinetics of the rod-derived retinal outputs originates largely from the rods themselves rather than from a light-dependent shift in the routing of rod signals through fast and slow retinal circuits.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: The speeding of rod-derived RGC responses can be explained by changes in the kinetics of phototransduction together with voltage-dependent changes in the conversion of outer segment currents to voltages.
source: Such effects, however, appear relatively minor as the speeding of rod-derived RGC responses can be explained by changes in the kinetics of phototransduction together with voltage-dependent changes in the conversion of outer segment currents to voltages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: The integration time of rod-derived RGC responses decreases by a factor of ~3 from low scotopic to high mesopic light levels.
source: Indeed, the integration time of rod-derived RGC responses decreases by a factor of ~3 from low scotopic to high mesopic light levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Retinal circuits integrate for relatively long times at low light levels, where detecting sparse photon absorptions is a primary challenge.
source: Retinal circuits integrate for relatively long times at low light levels, where detecting sparse photon absorptions is a primary challenge.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 8 and general principles of signal processing.

claim: At low light levels, signal-to-noise is improved ~2-fold compared to the situation with a fixed short integration time.
source: At low light levels, signal-to-noise is improved ~2-fold compared to the situation with a fixed short integration time.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The speeding of rod signals has been attributed to a shift in routing of rod signals from the (presumed slow) primary pathway to the (presumed fast) secondary or cone bipolar pathway.
source: The speeding of rod signals has been attributed to a shift in routing of rod signals from the (presumed slow) primary pathway to the (presumed fast) secondary or cone bipolar pathway.
evidence: This is a description of a hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Light-level-dependent changes in rod signaling in primate are not due to a change in routing, but instead to flexibility within the primary pathway.
source: This implies that light-level-dependent changes in rod signaling in primate, such as those illustrated in Figure 8, are not due to a change in routing, but instead to flexibility within the primary pathway.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Mouse rod bipolar cells make some contacts with cones.
source: Specifically, mouse rod bipolar cells, long thought to receive input exclusively from rods, make some contacts with cones (Behrens et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Mouse rod bipolar cells can convey cone-derived signals.
source: and can convey cone-derived signals (Pang et al., 2010; Szikra et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cone inputs to rod bipolar cells have not been observed in primate retina.
source: Cone inputs to rod bipolar cells have not been observed in primate retina.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of a finding in primate retina.

claim: Rod contacts on cone bipolar dendrites appear more numerous in mouse than primate.
source: Similarly, rod contacts on cone bipolar dendrites appear more numerous in mouse than primate (Tsukamoto and Omi, 2014; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: There is greater mixing of rod and cone signals in rodent retina than in primate retina.
source: This suggests a greater mixing of rod and cone signals in rodent retina than in primate retina.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical differences cited.

claim: The gap junctions between rods and cones convey at most a small rod-derived signal in primate retina.
source: Our work here shows a surprisingly clear separation of rod and cone signals in primate retina – with even the well-established gap junctions between rods and cones (Kolb, 1977; Hornstein et al., 2005) conveying at most a small rod-derived signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, with reference to previous anatomical work.

claim: The separation of rod and cone signals through most of the retinal circuitry maximizes opportunities for independent processing.
source: The resulting separation of rod and cone signals through most of the retinal circuitry maximizes opportunities for independent processing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding of signal separation.

claim: Independent processing of rod and cone signals may be particularly important under mesopic conditions when rod signals are approaching saturation and cone signals are small and threatened by noise.
source: Such independent processing may be particularly important under mesopic conditions when rod signals are approaching saturation and cone signals are small and threatened by noise.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Mechanistic studies derived from mouse may not be directly applicable to humans.
source: Our work also provides a cautionary reminder that mechanistic studies derived from mouse may not be directly applicable to humans.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the species differences observed.

claim: Neuromodulators could enhance rod signaling through the secondary pathway in vivo.
source: An issue of particular concern is the washout of neuromodulators that could enhance rod signaling through the secondary pathway – for example the dopaminergic signaling important in circadian rhythms (Ribelayga et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential limitations of the in vitro preparation, with reference to previous work.

claim: The same in vitro preparation does not eliminate the secondary pathway in mouse.
source: We note, however, that the same preparation does not eliminate the secondary pathway in mouse, but this issue is confounded by a lack of circadian regulation in C57/Bl6 mice (Jin and Ribelayga, 2016).
evidence: This is an observation from the study with reference to a potential confound.

claim: The physiological estimate of the upper end of primate rod signaling (300 R*/rod/s) agrees well with human perceptual results.
source: Our physiological estimate of the upper end of primate rod signaling agrees well with human perceptual results (Sharpe et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a comparison between the authors' data and perceptual data from the literature.

claim: Recordings from rodents reveal that rods can modulate retinal outputs at considerably higher light levels than suggested by short-term saturation measurements.
source: However, recordings from rodents reveal that rods can modulate retinal outputs at considerably higher light levels (Yin et al., 2006; Naarendorp et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work in rodents.

claim: Remaining rod responses at high light levels rely at least in part on a form of bleaching adaptation that allows rods to regain sensitivity after prolonged exposure (>10 min) to photopic backgrounds.
source: These remaining rod responses rely at least in part on a form of bleaching adaptation that allows rods to regain sensitivity after prolonged exposure (>10 min) to photopic backgrounds (Tikidji-Hamburyan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: On short time scales (≤10 min), rods could no longer modulate RGC output at backgrounds at or above 10^4 R*/rod/s in mouse.
source: On short time scales (≤10 min) and consistent with our results (Figure 4), Tikidji-Hamburyan and colleagues found that rods could no longer modulate RGC output at backgrounds at or above 104 R*/rod/s.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The 15 Hz rod flicker null was not observed in previous in vivo recordings from monkey parasol and midget RGCs.
source: This flicker null was similarly not observed in previous in vivo recordings from monkey parasol and midget RGCs (Cao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Interactions between rod and cone signals affect many aspects of mesopic vision.
source: Interactions between rod and cone signals affect many aspects of mesopic vision (reviewed by (Buck, 2014; Stockman and Sharpe, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Rod adaptation, and not rerouting, is the critical retinal mechanism that shapes the time course of rod-derived signals and ultimately human perception under scotopic and mesopic conditions.
source: Thus, this work implicates rod adaptation, and not rerouting, as the critical retinal mechanism that shapes the time course of rod-derived signals and ultimately human perception under scotopic and mesopic conditions.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Primate retinas were obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the Washington National Primate Research Center.
source: Retinas were obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the Washington National Primate Research Center
evidence: This is a methodological detail about tissue sourcing.

claim: All procedures followed protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Washington.
source: all procedures followed protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Washington.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Pieces of retina were dark-adapted for >1 hr before experiments.
source: In brief, pieces of retina attached to the pigment epithelium were stored in ~32–34° C oxygenated (95% O2/5% CO2) Ames medium (Sigma) and dark-adapted for >1 hr.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about tissue preparation.

claim: Psychophysical measurements of rod vision in humans indicate that dark adaptation is near complete in 30–45 min.
source: Psychophysical measurements of rod vision in humans indicate that dark adaptation is near complete in 30–45 min (Sharpe et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to perceptual work.

claim: Isolated primate retinas were dark-adapted for ≥1 hr before any data was collected.
source: Thus, isolated primate retinas (attached to the pigment epithelium) were dark-adapted for ≥1 hr before any data was collected.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Mice were dark adapted for ≥12 hr before isolating the retina.
source: Mice were dark adapted for ≥12 hr before isolating the retina.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.
